name: marker-interface
intent: Mark a type as belonging to a category by having it declare an empty marker type, so that code can recognise the category through the type system at compile time or through a type test at run time without imposing any member to implement.
problem: A capability or category must be recognisable across otherwise unrelated types, but there is no behaviour to attach to it: forcing a method, a base class or a shared supertype merely to carry the mark distorts the hierarchy and invents a contract nobody can implement meaningfully.
context: Languages and codebases that expose nominal subtyping or run-time type information (Java interfaces, C# interfaces, Rust traits, Swift protocols, Ruby modules, C++ RTTI) and need a boolean fact about a type - serializable, deletable, random-access, sendable, retryable - consumed by a framework, a generic bound or a dispatch routine. The mark is a decision about the type system, not about object state: it is chosen when the fact is intrinsic to the type and stable for all of its instances.
benefits: Recognition is part of the type system: generic bounds, method signatures and pattern matches can require the mark, so misuse is caught at compile time where an annotation would only fail at run time.
No member, no state and no superclass is imposed on marked types - classes that share nothing else can join the category.
Subtypes inherit the mark automatically, so a whole hierarchy is recognised by one declaration and one test.
Run-time recognition is a constant-time type test (instanceof, is, type switch) and in Rust/Swift can be free of run-time cost entirely.
Markers compose: a type can carry several marks, which annotations cannot express as a type relationship in most languages.
Names a cross-cutting concept (Serializable, RandomAccess, Deletable) without inventing an artificial base class or a dummy method.
tradeoffs: The mark cannot be unimplemented: every subclass inherits it, so opting out needs a runtime workaround (Java serialization forces such subclasses to throw NotSerializableException).
It swaps the interface's usual meaning - a behavioural contract - for metadata about a type, which several style guides treat as abuse (C# CA1040, Essential C#).
The compiler checks the mark, never the property it denotes: a class marked serializable or thread-safe can still be a lie, and the failure surfaces at run time.
Adding a mark to a public type silently retags every existing subtype and can change behaviour of code you do not own, including dispatch that inspects the mark.
Markers are all-or-nothing: they cannot carry values or parameters, and they cannot annotate methods, fields or parameters - annotations or tag objects are needed for that.
Empty types are easy to misread: without a documented consumer a marker interface looks like an unfinished design or a default supertype.

participants.responsibility: The empty interface, trait, protocol or module that names the category; it declares no members and exists only to be implemented.
A class, struct or enum that declares conformance to the marker, advertising the category to the whole program and to all of its subtypes.
The framework, generic bound, serializer or dispatch routine that tests for the mark - through a compile-time constraint or a run-time type test - and performs the category-specific behaviour.
The compiler, runtime or annotation processor that records and evaluates the mark and decides what conforming to it means (inheritance, bootstrapping, auto-implementation).

use_cases: Serialization eligibility: java.io.Serializable marks classes whose state ObjectOutputStream may write; .NET uses the [Serializable] attribute for the same signal.
Algorithm selection: java.util.RandomAccess marks lists with fast indexed access so Collections algorithms choose the indexed loop instead of the iterator loop.
Capability gates in domain APIs: a Deletable or Retryable marker lets a repository or command executor accept only declared-eligible objects, and `where T : IDeletable` enforces it at compile time.
Framework recognition of participating classes: ASP.NET session-state markers (IRequiresSessionState) and RMI's java.rmi.Remote mark types for framework treatment without adding members.
Concurrency facts: Rust's Send/Sync, Swift's Sendable and thread-safety markers tell generic and concurrent code which types may cross an execution boundary.
Test and tooling markers: runners and fixtures mark classes so they can be discovered (xUnit-style attribute/interface marking in test frameworks).
Cloud event and protocol markers: AWS SDKs, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, and CloudEvents specification use marker types to categorise payload shapes (e.g., CloudEvent-specific serialisation requirements).

Domain-Driven Design type categorization: DDD tactical patterns use marker interfaces to distinguish Entities, Value Objects, Aggregates, and Domain Events from plain domain objects, especially in languages without built-in category types.

Persistence framework recognition: JPA (Java) uses @Entity and @Embeddable as annotations, but Spring Data REST and Hibernate validator use marker interfaces for repository discovery and validation group routing.
GraphQL schema type markers: schema-first GraphQL libraries use marker interfaces to tag types as Query, Mutation, or Subscription roots for code generation.
Protocol-buffer and RPC code generation: protobuf-lite and gRPC stubs use generated marker interfaces to mark service clients vs. server implementations.
Security capability markers: Spring Security's SecurityMarker interface and Jakarta EE's @RolesAllowed on method-level contrast with type-level security role markers used to gate method dispatch.

Rust concurrency contracts: Rust's `std::marker::Send` and `Sync` are marker traits; the compiler auto-implements them when safe, and generic or thread APIs use bounds to permit transfer or shared references across threads.

Swift structured concurrency: the standard library's `Sendable` protocol has no required members, yet compiler-enforced conformance allows values across concurrency domains; `@unchecked Sendable` makes the author's proof obligation explicit.
avoid_when: The signal is descriptive metadata, may carry values, or must apply to fields, methods or parameters - use an annotation or attribute (Effective Java Item 41).
The property can be checked structurally - duck typing, respond_to?, a runtime-checkable protocol, a C++ concept - so nominal conformance adds a declaration without adding enforcement.
A method can express the contract meaningfully, or the 'capability' is really behaviour - declare the method instead of an empty type.
The marked set is closed and small - a sealed hierarchy or enum with exhaustive matching documents and checks it better.
The language ecosystem already provides the mark (Serializable, Sendable, IDisposable-style interfaces) or the fact is configuration rather than a stable property of the type.
anti_patterns: Empty interface used as a default supertype to group unrelated classes 'for reuse', with no consumer that ever tests the mark.
Hybrid marker-plus-contract interfaces that silently carry one or two methods, leaving readers unsure whether conformance is a fact or a capability.
Marking a class as capable (serializable, cloneable, thread-safe) when the conformance is not actually true - the compiler cannot check the claim, so the lie ships.
A marker whose only consumer was deleted; the empty interface survives as a dangling tag that still constrains subclasses and misleads readers.
Replacing a real behavioural interface with a marker plus reflection-based dispatch to the methods that used to live on the interface.
design_principles: Nominal typing as a design tool: state facts in the type system so the compiler can enforce them.
Separation of concerns: a type's metadata facts are declared separately from the behaviour that consumes them.
Open/closed principle: new types join the category by declaring conformance; consumers stay closed for modification.
Least commitment: the mark imposes no members, no state and no superclass on participating types.
Documented intent: every mark names both its meaning and the code that reads it.
best_practices: Name the signal precisely (RetryableCommand, not SpecialCommand) and document who reads the mark and what happens when it is present.
Keep markers empty; if a method is needed, declare a real interface and relate the marker to it deliberately instead of growing the marker.
Prefer a compile-time consumer (generic bound, concept, sealed set) over run-time reflection whenever the language allows, because only then is the mark enforced.
Use annotations or attributes instead when the signal is descriptive, carries values, or applies to anything other than a type.
Treat a public marker as a published contract: adding or removing one changes the type relationship for all existing subtypes.
Do not mark what you cannot guarantee - make the promise the mark makes true by construction, by tests, or by narrowing what the mark means.
In .NET, apply [SuppressMessage] with a justification comment when CA1040 fires for a deliberate compile-time marker - document why a runtime attribute is insufficient.
In Java, prefer marker interfaces over marker annotations when the mark must constrain a generic type parameter (e.g., <T extends Serializable>) or when framework compatibility requires an interface.

In languages with both (Java, Kotlin, C#), prefer annotation/attribute when the mark is purely descriptive, searchable at runtime via reflection, or applies to method/field level; prefer marker interface when compile-time enforcement or type-bound polymorphism is needed.
Document the consumer of the marker explicitly in the Javadoc/KDoc/XML doc - a marker without a known reader is technical debt.

In TypeScript (structural typing), simulate a nominal marker by exporting a unique symbol type and using intersection types: type Marked = { readonly _brand: unique symbol } - this prevents accidental structural matching.
Prefer sealed class hierarchies over marker interfaces when the set of categories is closed and known at compile time; the compiler enforces exhaustiveness where a marker only names a subset.
For multi-axis markers (e.g., both Persistent and Auditable), prefer separate markers over one marker with flags to keep each concern orthogonal and independently testable.
Version marker interfaces conservatively: treat adding a marker to a public type as a potentially breaking change, especially in library code, because all existing subtypes silently inherit it.
sources: Joshua Bloch, Effective Java, 3rd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2018), Item 41: Use marker interfaces to define types.

pitfalls: Marking every type 'just in case' turns the marker into a default supertype that no consumer ever reads.
A mark whose claim the compiler cannot check (serializable, thread-safe) can be a lie; only mark what holds for every instance and subtype.
Hybrid markers that also declare methods blur the boundary between metadata and behavioural contract.

In TypeScript's structural type system, any type with the same shape as a marker interface is assignable to it - use unique-symbol or branded types for genuine nominal markers, otherwise the mark has no effect.

In Java, Cloneable and Serializable are notorious legacy markers whose claims are not enforced by the compiler; always validate with explicit tests and documented preconditions rather than relying on the mark alone.
Marker interfaces with no documented consumer survive as dangling design artefacts that constrain subtypes and mislead future readers - always pair a marker with its consumer.
Adding a marker to a library type silently propagates it to all implementing subclasses; in API libraries this can change dispatch behaviour in client code unexpectedly - version conservatively.

Confusing annotation/attribute with marker interface in languages that support both leads to inconsistent designs where some capabilities are runtime-only and others are compile-time - establish a team convention.

related_patterns_notes.interface-class: The interface-class pairing provides the abstract interface that a marker interface's consumer can bind against; marker interfaces are often the degenerate case of an interface class with zero operations.
related_patterns_notes.extension-interface: Extension interface (POSA2) allows a component to expose multiple named interfaces to avoid bloat; unlike marker interfaces, each extension interface carries behaviour. Both patterns share the goal of tagging a type for a particular consumer.
related_patterns_notes.role-object: Role object separates a behavioural role from the primary object hierarchy; a marker interface can tag which role(s) a class plays, serving as the entry point to role-based design without inheriting from a fixed hierarchy.
related_patterns_notes.tag-dispatching: Tag dispatch selects algorithm variants based on type tags; marker interfaces are the canonical source of those tags in OO languages. Unlike ad-hoc tag fields, a marker interface is inherited and composable.
related_patterns_notes.layer-supertype: Layer supertype concentrates common behaviour in an abstract base class; a marker interface can be applied to all subtypes of a layer-supertype hierarchy as a category signal without adding shared state.
related_patterns_notes.intention-revealing-interface: Intention-revealing interface names what a type does rather than what it is; a marker interface is the purest form of intention-revealing type naming when the intention is a capability category.
related_patterns_notes.sealed-hierarchy: When the set of categories is closed, sealed classes/interfaces enforce exhaustiveness at compile time and eliminate the need for a marker interface to recognise categories - prefer sealed hierarchies when the set is known and stable. sealed-hierarchy
related_patterns_notes.marker-annotation: Marker annotation is the annotation/attribute equivalent of a marker interface - languages that support both should use marker interface when compile-time constraints or generic bounds are needed; marker annotation when the signal is descriptive, runtime-readable, or applies beyond types. marker-annotation
